What exactly is fructose?

blocks.x: Fructose is a simple 6-carbon sugar — specifically a polyhydroxyketone, making it a structural isomer of glucose (same formula, different shape). It occurs naturally in honey, tree and vine fruits, flowers, berries, and most root vegetables, and commercially it's usually extracted from sugar cane, sugar beets, or corn.

When you chew on a stick of sugarcane, you're tasting sucrose — a disaccharide made of one glucose and one fructose joined together. Sucrose is actually the major dietary source of fructose. Once digested, free fructose is absorbed directly into the bloodstream during digestion — no waiting around required.

A key difference from glucose: fructose's entry into cells is not controlled by insulin. This matters a lot, because glucose's entry into most tissues is tightly regulated by insulin, while fructose slips in regardless of the insulin signal.

sections.title: Why does fructose get its own name for breakdown?

blocks.x: Fructolysis refers specifically to how fructose from the diet is metabolized. Unlike glucose, which is used all over the body, fructose is metabolized almost completely in the liver.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — the specialized cocoa processing plant

blocks.x: Imagine raw cocoa beans harvested across the country, but there's only one specific factory equipped to process them into usable cocoa products — everything gets routed there. That's fructose and the liver: almost every gram of dietary fructose is funneled specifically into liver cells for processing, unlike glucose which can be "processed" by nearly every tissue in the body.
Fructose and glucose metabolism share many of the same chemical intermediates along the way — but their fates differ sharply.
Fructose is directed mainly toward replenishing liver glycogen and de novo lipogenesis (making new fatty acids/triglycerides) — rather than being burned everywhere for general energy like glucose.
Fructose transport into cells is slower than glucose transport, and fructose uptake does not stimulate insulin secretion at all.

blocks.cap: Fructose is trapped, then split into two 3-carbon pieces that funnel into familiar territory.

blocks.x: Fructokinase (found in liver, kidney, and intestine) phosphorylates fructose to fructose-1-phosphate, trapping it inside the cell for metabolism. Hexokinase can also phosphorylate fructose to fructose-6-phosphate, but it has low affinity for fructose, so this is only a minor backup route. Essentially all fructose in the human liver becomes fructose-1-phosphate.
Fructose-1-phosphate aldolase (aldolase B) hydrolyzes fructose-1-phosphate into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glyceraldehyde.

items.title: Step 3 — Both pieces rejoin familiar pathways

blocks.x: DHAP can be isomerized to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (by triosephosphate isomerase) or reduced to glycerol-3-phosphate. The glyceraldehyde piece can be converted to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (by glyceraldehyde kinase) or to glycerol-3-phosphate. From here, intermediates can feed glycogen synthesis, be oxidized to pyruvate, or reduced to lactate.

blocks.title: Why fructose metabolizes so fast — and why that's a problem

blocks.x: Glycolysis has a built-in speed bump: the rate-limiting, tightly regulated enzyme phosphofructokinase (PFK-1). Fructose metabolism completely bypasses this checkpoint by entering the pathway further downstream. It's like a delivery truck skipping the weigh-station checkpoint that all other trucks must pass through — it moves through faster and largely unregulated. The result: high dietary fructose intake sharply increases acetyl-CoA production and lipogenesis (fatty acid, triglyceride, and VLDL synthesis) — because there's no checkpoint slowing the flow down.

sections.title: An alternate recipe: turning glucose into fructose

blocks.x: The polyol (sorbitol) pathway converts glucose to fructose using sorbitol as a go-between. This pathway is absent in the liver, but present in the lens and retina of the eye, kidney, placenta, Schwann cells of peripheral nerves, erythrocytes, and seminal vesicles.

blocks.cap: Two enzymes, one detour: glucose → sorbitol → fructose.

blocks.title: Why bother? Fructose is sperm's favourite fuel

blocks.x: In the seminal vesicles, this exact pathway converts glucose to fructose, which is then secreted in semen as the preferred fuel for sperm cells — a clever, dedicated production line for one very specific purpose.

blocks.title: When it goes wrong — diabetes and cataracts

blocks.x: In uncontrolled diabetes (hyperglycemia), a flood of glucose enters insulin-independent cells like those in the lens, retina, nerves, and kidney. These tissues have plenty of aldose reductase and NADPH, so glucose is rapidly converted to sorbitol. But sorbitol dehydrogenase is low or absent in these same cells — so sorbitol doesn't get converted onward to fructose. Since sorbitol can't easily cross the cell membrane, it accumulates, and being water-attracting (hydrophilic), it draws in water by osmosis, swelling the cell. Analogy: like floodwater pouring into a compound during heavy rains with no drainage outlet — it just keeps rising, and the swelling pressure damages everything inside. This sorbitol build-up is linked to diabetic complications like cataracts, peripheral neuropathy, and nephropathy.

sections.title: Two very different genetic conditions — one harmless, one serious

blocks.x: Caused by a deficiency in hepatic fructokinase (autosomal recessive). Fructose can't be phosphorylated to fructose-1-phosphate, so it's never trapped inside liver cells — it simply leaks back into the blood, and once plasma levels exceed the kidney's reabsorption threshold, fructose spills into the urine (fructosuria). It's a benign, asymptomatic condition with no treatment needed — the amount lost in urine is small and depends only on dietary fructose intake.

items.title: Hereditary Fructose Intolerance — the serious one

blocks.x: Caused by absence of aldolase B (fructose-1-phosphate aldolase). Fructose gets trapped as fructose-1-phosphate but can't go any further. It piles up in the liver, kidney, and small intestine, trapping the cell's phosphate supply — phosphate that's needed to activate glycogen phosphorylase (which releases glucose from glycogen). This blocks both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, causing severe hypoglycemia. Ingesting fructose can trigger vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, kidney failure, haemorrhage, and hyperuricemia. Treatment: a strict fructose-free diet, which carries a good prognosis if followed.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a missing exit vs. a total gridlock

blocks.x: Essential fructosuria is like a road with one missing exit ramp — traffic (fructose) just continues past and eventually spills out somewhere harmless (the urine). Hereditary fructose intolerance is like a total gridlock on the main highway — vehicles (fructose-1-phosphate) pile up so badly that they block the roads needed for completely different traffic (glucose release from glycogen), bringing much bigger parts of the system to a halt.

sections.title: Why can too much soft drink lead to gout?

blocks.x: Even in people with completely normal enzymes, very high fructose consumption can cause problems. Because fructokinase rapidly converts fructose to fructose-1-phosphate, but aldolase B's activity is comparatively limited, fructose-1-phosphate can build up faster than it's cleared — even in healthy livers, if intake is high enough.

blocks.cap: The chain reaction from excess fructose intake to elevated uric acid levels.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — hoarding during a scarcity

blocks.x: When fructose-1-phosphate binds up (sequesters) the cell's limited supply of inorganic phosphate (Pi), it's like one trader hoarding all the available fuel during a fuel scarcity — everyone else who genuinely needs that fuel (like ATP synthesis, which requires ADP + Pi) is left without. With less Pi around, ATP production drops, and the cell starts breaking down ADP and AMP instead — a breakdown pathway that ends in uric acid. Sustained high fructose intake over a long period is linked to elevated blood uric acid and increased risk of gout.

sections.title: What exactly is galactose?

blocks.x: Galactose is a monosaccharide that, when joined with glucose, forms lactose — the sugar found in milk. The enzyme lactase (β-galactosidase), found in intestinal mucosal cells, hydrolyzes lactose into free glucose and galactose.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — breast milk and baby formula

blocks.x: Every breastfeeding baby is running on lactose as a major fuel source — lactase in their gut splits it into glucose and galactose for absorption. Like fructose, galactose's entry into cells is not dependent on insulin. Beyond dairy, galactose is found in sugar beets, gums, and mucilages, and the body also makes its own galactose as part of glycolipids and glycoproteins in various tissues.

The only way the body can break down (catabolize) galactose is by converting it to glucose — a relatively slow process that happens only in the liver. Because of this, the liver's ability to convert galactose to glucose can even be used as a clinical liver function test.

blocks.cap: Galactose converted step by step into a form glucose metabolism can use directly.

blocks.x: Galactose is phosphorylated to galactose-1-phosphate, with ATP as the phosphate donor (and Mg²⁺ as cofactor).

Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase swaps galactose-1-phosphate onto UDP-glucose, forming UDP-galactose and releasing glucose-1-phosphate — which can either feed glycogen synthesis or be converted by phosphoglucomutase to glucose-6-phosphate (which can enter glycolysis, or be converted to free glucose by glucose-6-phosphatase).

UDP-galactose 4-epimerase converts UDP-galactose back into UDP-glucose, ready to accept another galactose-1-phosphate. This makes UDP-glucose act almost like a reusable coenzyme in this cycle — never permanently consumed.

sections.title: A minor pothole vs. a major bridge collapse

blocks.x: Autosomal recessive; galactose can't be converted to galactose-1-phosphate, so it (and its byproduct galactitol) accumulates instead. The main clinical sign is cataracts, developing within the first weeks or months of life — caused by galactitol accumulating in the eye lens, drawing in water osmotically (galactitol can't leave the lens), and causing swelling damage. Aside from the eyes, this condition is relatively contained.

Caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase — a rare, autosomal recessive congenital disease. Galactose metabolism is broadly impaired, raising galactose levels in blood (galactosemia) and urine (galactosuria). Accumulated galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol damage multiple tissues — liver, nervous system, lens, and kidney — causing weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, mental retardation, and in severe cases cataracts, amino aciduria, and albuminuria. Diagnosis is by measuring transferase activity in erythrocytes; treatment is a strict galactose- and lactose-free diet.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a minor pothole vs. a major bridge collapse

blocks.x: Galactokinase deficiency is like a single pothole on a side street — annoying and locally damaging (mainly the eyes), but the rest of the city's traffic flows fine. Classical galactosemia is like a major bridge collapsing on the main route — it disrupts transport to and from multiple districts (liver, brain, kidney, eyes) all at once, which is why its effects are so much more severe and widespread.

sections.title: Key takeaways

items: Fructose enters cells insulin-independently via GLUT5 (gut) and GLUT2 (blood/liver), and is metabolized almost entirely in the liver via fructokinase and aldolase B.
Fructose metabolism bypasses PFK-1, glycolysis's main checkpoint — which is why high fructose intake drives fat synthesis so effectively.
The polyol pathway converts glucose to fructose via sorbitol; in diabetes, sorbitol build-up in insulin-independent tissues (eye, nerves, kidney) contributes to cataracts and neuropathy.
Essential fructosuria (fructokinase deficiency) is benign; hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency) is serious, causing severe hypoglycemia after fructose ingestion.
Excess fructose intake can sequester phosphate, lowering ATP synthesis and raising uric acid — a pathway linked to gout.
Galactose, from lactose, is converted to glucose only in the liver, via galactokinase, galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase, and UDP-galactose-4-epimerase.
Galactokinase deficiency mainly causes cataracts; classical galactosemia (transferase deficiency) is far more severe, affecting the liver, brain, kidney, and eyes.

items.d: Fructose enters cells via GLUT5, insulin-independent.
Fructose-1-P splits into DHAP + glyceraldehyde, which feed into glycolysis.
Galactose-1-P swaps with UDP-glucose to form UDP-galactose + Glucose-1-P.
UDP-galactose ↔ UDP-glucose, allowing entry into glycolysis/glycogenesis.
